ox: Correct. Acidity depends on how stable the conjugate base is. Acetate's negative charge is spread (delocalized) over two oxygens by resonance; ethoxide has its charge stuck on one oxygen. The more stable base means the stronger acid.
Incorrect. A STRONGER O–H bond would make acetic acid harder to ionize, not easier. Bond strength is not the main factor here.
Incorrect. The number of hydrogens does not matter. Only the one acidic hydrogen leaves, and what matters is the stability of what is left behind.
Incorrect. Ethoxide has no resonance stabilization: the methyl group has no π system to share charge with. Resonance is exactly what ethoxide LACKS.

concept.t: Why carboxylic acids are stronger acids than alcohols
p: A stronger acid is one whose conjugate base is more stable. Resonance is one of the four stability factors (Atom, Resonance, Induction, Orbital). Acetate delocalizes its charge across two oxygens; ethoxide cannot. Acetic acid (pKa ≈ 4.8) is about 10¹¹ times more acidic than ethanol (pKa ≈ 16).

x5B_027.trap: Picking bond strength: a stronger O–H bond would make the acid weaker, not stronger.
x5B_027.eli: A spread-out charge is a happy charge. Acetate shares its negative charge between two oxygens like two friends carrying one heavy bag; ethoxide carries it alone.
mem: Stronger acid = more stable conjugate base.
ARIO order of stability factors: Atom, Resonance, Induction, Orbital.
pKa guide: carboxylic acid ≈ 4–5, phenol ≈ 10, alcohol ≈ 16.
x5B_027.sc: Draw the conjugate base. If you can draw a second resonance structure, that acid is stronger.
x5B_027.mn: ARIO: A = Atom (size/electronegativity), R = Resonance, I = Induction, O = Orbital (s-character).
